title: Broadcasting Internet Datagrams in the Presence of Subnets
summary: This RFC extends the broadcasting rules in RFC 919 to networks that are divided into subnets. It proposes how to address broadcasts and how gateways should handle them when subnets are present.

eli5.summary: The shout-to-the-room rules needed updating for neighborhoods split into smaller streets, so this note says how to shout to one street or to all.

questions: how do ip broadcasts work with subnets
how to address broadcasts to a subnet
how does ip broadcast work with subnets
subtitle: How to address and forward IP broadcasts when a network is split into subnets, using all-ones numbers and Reverse Path Forwarding.

tldr.problem: Broadcasting is not covered by the basic IP specification, and the arrival of subnets makes it unclear how to say 'everyone on this network' or how gateways should pass such datagrams along without creating loops.
tldr.mechanism: A host-number or subnet-number field of all ones means broadcast, and gateways follow simple rules: never rebroadcast on the network a datagram arrived from, and for all-subnets broadcasts use Reverse Path Forwarding.
tldr.outcome: The memo is an Internet Standard and has not been obsoleted. It gives hosts a way to broadcast without knowing whether a network is subnetted.

facts.label: All-hosts value
facts.value: Host number with all bits one

facts.label: All-subnets value
facts.value: Subnet number with all bits one

today: RFC 922 is an Internet Standard and the metadata lists no replacement, so it stands as published. It extends the broadcasting rules of RFC 919 for networks divided into subnets.

sections.title: Why Broadcast, and Why Rules Are Needed
sections.content:
RFC 922 proposes simple rules for broadcasting Internet datagrams on local networks that support broadcast, for addressing those broadcasts, and for how gateways should handle them. The basic IP specification (RFC 791) does not cover broadcasting, so there was no agreed way to do it and protocol designers had not made use of it.

The memo considers only unreliable, unsequenced and possibly duplicated datagram broadcasts. It assumes the data link layer supports efficient broadcasting, but not that broadcasts are reliably delivered: a host should receive most of them. Because every host that hears a broadcast spends some effort on it, broadcasting should be used only when it is the best solution to a problem.

Broadcasts help when a host needs information without knowing which host can supply it, or wants to give information to many hosts quickly. The RFC contrasts this with wired-in lists of neighbors, which are inflexible, and with polling all plausible host numbers, which is slow (it notes roughly 65 thousand plausible host numbers on the ARPANET).
sections.eli5: Shouting is a quick way to find someone when you do not know who has the answer. But everyone has to stop and listen, so you should only shout when you really need to.

sections.title: Hardware Networks, IP Networks and Subnets
sections.content:
Broadcasting depends on the data link layer, so the RFC separates physical from logical networks. Seen from a sending or forwarding host, the local hardware network is the physical link it is attached to, and a remote hardware network is one separated from it by at least one gateway.

An IP network is one hardware network or a collection of them sharing one IP network number. A subnet is a single member of that collection. Hosts on different subnets share the network number, and the local-address part is divided into a subnet number and a host number. The RFC does not assume any particular division. It admits that adding a subnet level is at variance with the IP specification, but expects subnetting to spread. From the point of view of a host on another IP network, it should not matter whether an IP network is one hardware network or many subnets.
sections.eli5: A town (the IP network) can have many streets (subnets). Houses on every street share the town name, but each house also has a street number and a house number.

sections.title: Classes of Broadcast
sections.content:
The RFC lists several kinds of IP broadcasting.

  • Single-destination datagram broadcast on the local net: the datagram is for one host, but the sender broadcasts it at the data link layer, perhaps to avoid routing. This is not an IP broadcast, and a host should discard a datagram not meant for it without printing an error.
  • Local hardware net broadcast: a distinguished host-number value means all hosts. This is the most useful case. It lets a host discover gateways without wired-in tables and is the basis for address resolution protocols.
  • Directed broadcast to a remote hardware network: the datagram is routed normally until it reaches a gateway attached to the destination network, which then broadcasts it. The RFC also calls this a 'letter bomb'.
  • Multi-subnet broadcast: a distinguished subnet-number value means all subnets of a subnetted IP network.
  • Broadcast to the entire Internet: probably not useful and almost certainly not desirable.

For reasons of performance or security, a gateway may choose not to forward broadcasts, and banning broadcasts into or out of an autonomous group of networks may be a good idea.
sections.eli5: You can whisper to one person, shout to one room, shout into another room through a helper, or shout to a whole building. Shouting to the entire world is a bad idea.

sections.title: How Hosts and Gateways Handle Broadcasts
sections.content:
A host's IP receiving layer must be modified so that it compares a datagram's destination not only with the host's own addresses but also with the broadcast addresses that apply to it. To send a local or directed broadcast, a host just uses the right destination address and sends as usual; any sophisticated algorithm needs to live only in gateways.

For a local broadcast, a gateway follows these rules in order. The primary loop-avoidance rule is never broadcast a datagram on the hardware network it was received on. Merely ignoring datagrams the gateway itself sent is not enough when several gateways share a network.

  • If the datagram arrived on the network it is addressed to, do not forward it, but treat the gateway as one of its destinations.
  • Otherwise, if it is addressed to a hardware network the gateway is connected to, send it as a data link broadcast there, and again count as a destination.
  • Otherwise, use normal routing to pick the next gateway.

A directed broadcast for a network the gateway is not connected to is simply forwarded the usual way.
sections.eli5: A helper who hears a shout may pass it to the right street, but must never shout it back onto the street it came from, or the shout would bounce around forever.

sections.title: Reverse Path Forwarding for All-Subnets Broadcasts
sections.content:
The hardest case is a broadcast to every subnet of an IP network. The RFC says the best method it knows is Reverse Path Forwarding (RPF). It is suboptimal in cost and reliability but quite good, extremely simple, and needs no additional data space in a gateway. The criteria for a good method include no change to the IP datagram format, reasonable efficiency, minimal gateway modification and a high likelihood of delivery.

The rule is: a gateway forwards copies of the datagram along all connected links if and only if the datagram arrived on the link that is part of the best route between the gateway and the source of the datagram. Otherwise it discards the datagram as a duplicate. Non-gateway hosts need no extra complexity. The RFC notes the method can be improved if gateways exchange additional information.

The memo also gives a pseudo-Algol routing procedure for gateways (its Figure 1). It checks whether the destination network is directly attached, whether it is subnetted, and whether the subnet or host part is the broadcast value. Depending on the answer it forwards, examines the packet for the gateway's own use, or discards it to avoid a loop.
sections.eli5: Each helper passes the shout on only if it came from the direction of the shortest road back to the person who first shouted. Copies that arrive some other way are thrown away, so the shout spreads out without circling back.

sections.title: Broadcast Address Conventions
sections.content:
For different implementations to interoperate, there must be a convention for 'all hosts' and 'all subnets'. The RFC picks a number whose bits are all ones for both, because it is unlikely to belong to a real host (this assignment was first proposed in IEN-212). Using all ones for 'all subnets' too means a sender does not need to know how the destination address is divided into subnet and host fields, or whether it is divided at all.

The address 255.255.255.255 is a broadcast on the local hardware network that must not be forwarded. It can be used by hosts that do not know their network number and are asking a server for it. As an example, a host on net 36 can reach all of its neighbors with 255.255.255.255 and all of net 36 with 36.255.255.255, without knowing whether the net is subnetted. A robust application might try the first and, if there is no response, try the second.

All zeros could be read as 'unspecified'. The RFC says it probably has no reason to appear except as the source address of an ICMP Information Request. As a notation, a network is written with zero fields, so 36.0.0.0 means network number 36.
sections.eli5: A special house number made only of the biggest digits means 'everybody'. Because nobody lives at that number, it is safe to use for shouting to all.

sections.title: ARP Servers and Broadcast Loops
sections.content:
The RFC warns about the Address Resolution Protocol (RFC 826). On a network where not all hosts agree on what the broadcast address is, an ARP server could be tempted to map the IP broadcast address to the hardware broadcast address. The RFC says this temptation must be resisted: an ARP server should never respond to a request whose target is a broadcast address.

Such a request can only come from a host that does not recognize the broadcast address, and answering would almost certainly cause a forwarding loop. If N hosts on the physical network do not recognize the address as broadcast, a datagram with a Time-To-Live of T could give rise to T**N spurious re-broadcasts.

The memo has no dedicated security section. Apart from this warning, it only notes that a gateway may refuse to forward broadcasts for performance or security reasons.
sections.eli5: If a helper wrongly tells confused people where to send a shout, the shout can multiply as it bounces between them. So the helper must stay silent about that.

items.label: Local broadcast
items.desc: Broadcast on the local hardware network; must not be forwarded.

items.label: All hosts of net 36
items.desc: One hardware network, or all subnets of a subnetted network, whatever the split.

items.label: Network 36
items.desc: Zero fields name a network rather than a host.
